pixels.lens: Pixels and instrument: is it a real point source at a fixed place on the sky, and is it measured correctly? Own code (astropy, numpy, scipy) on all 425 cached cutouts of all six detectors. I also fetched 150 D5/D6 cutouts, 0.34 deg wide, centred on the bright star V345 Nor, from the public S3 bucket.

findings.what: Reality is not in doubt, but the spectrum points to a classical nova, so novelty is the open question. The light is dominated by hydrogen emission lines with very large equivalent widths (Pa alpha channel 9x the continuum, Br alpha 5x, Pf beta 3-4x, Br beta 3x, Pa beta 3x, Br gamma 2x). D1 detects the source only in the 1.08 um channel (He I 1.083 / Pa gamma), on its 6 clean core pixels; that aperture also holds PERSIST-flagged pixels, so this one is tentative. In Aug 2026 the continuum has faded but a line at 4.49 um is strong (possibly [Mg IV] 4.487 um, a nova coronal line; my identification is tentative). This fits a heavily reddened nova better than a young-star flare. The catalogue/report lens must check Galactic nova lists from Aug 2025 to Feb 2026 at this position. My lens cannot exclude that it is already reported.

findings.what: Several quoted numbers are misleading, though the conclusion stands. (1) The tile images' 178 and 300 mJy fall on emission features (4.739 um bump and Pf beta 4.631 um); the 4.4-5.0 um continuum is about 105 mJy. (2) The faint-state aperture values (D6 3.9/8.0, D5 8.4/12.3, D3 8.5 mJy) are light from neighbours inside the 15.4 arcsec aperture. Fitting the candidate with 28 catalogued neighbours modelled gives -0.5 +/- 0.1 mJy in D6 in Jul-Aug 2025. (3) 'Back to nearly nothing by Aug 2026' is wrong for the lines.

April 2026 data are partly spoiled by cosmic-ray/snowball patches, but the source was still there at about a third of its Feb-Mar level. The two D6 April exposures carry TRANSIENT/HALO/SNOWBALL flags on or next to the core (NSNOWSRC 21 and 251 in those images). One D6 value comes from only 3 clean core pixels; the other D6 exposure has none.

findings.what: It is one fixed place on the sky. The centroid holds still while the source crosses the detectors and under both spacecraft orientations. There is no motion and no wavelength-dependent shift: line channels and continuum channels give the same position.

findings.what: It is not a ghost of the 607 Jy Mira V345 Nor, 7.7 arcmin north (AllWISE W2 -1.37). The candidate appears only at the roll where V345 Nor sits about 74 px from it in +y, so the ghost test was needed. A ghost fixed in detector pixels would put at least 60 mJy at the mirrored place 7.7 arcmin north of the star in Jul-Aug 2025 and Jul-Sep 2026; nothing extra is there. A constant field star near that place has the same brightness in every visit. V345 Nor itself changed by at most a factor 1.6. Seeing the source at the same sky place under both orientations (Aug 2026 lines) rules out any fixed-offset ghost of any star. Seeing it fixed while it crosses the detector rules out ghosts that move with field position.
findings.evidence: ghost_test3.py: excess at each faint exposure's own predicted ghost place, compared with the same sky place in Feb-Mar: D6 -0.5 (MAD 2.2, n 18) and -0.9 (2.0, n 21) mJy; D5 -0.8 (2.6, n 12) and -0.3 (1.9, n 17). At the candidate: +103.4 (D6) and +117.2 (D5). ghost_test2: the field star there is 36-38 mJy in D6 in all four visits. mira.py, V345 Nor wing ring 9.5-12.5 px, D6: 1269 / 1600 / 1389 mJy. wide.png.

findings.what: Paired detectors agree at the same instant. Every D3/D6 exposure pair (18) sees the source in both detectors in the same 114 s exposure. The bright 'spikes' are spectral lines, not time flares or glitches: in a pair, the line is in one member while the other stays at continuum. Comparison stars are normal in the spike exposures. Line excesses fall at hydrogen wavelengths in 5 detectors and at very different detector rows (D4: 2.595 um at row 1697 and 3.700 um at row 162).

findings.what: Not persistence, crosstalk or saturation. The source keeps its sky place while its detector row changes by about 115 px per exposure, so it is not a latent image at fixed pixels. No CROSSTALK flag is set, and crosstalk would sit on V345 Nor's own rows, 74 rows away. The continuum is far below saturation. One channel is saturated: D5 at 4.040 um (Br alpha), with OVERFLOW+SUR_ERROR+BLOOM in the core; its aperture value of 331 mJy is a lower limit. The 4.075 um channel carries an OVERFLOW pixel, a valid partial reading per the Explanatory Supplement.
findings.evidence: measurements.json: flags and detector (x, y) per exposure; 2026W09_2A_0120_2 D5 is the only 'saturated' status in 425 exposures.

findings.what: The faint state is a real measurement, not a failure to measure. Jul-Aug 2025 has 19-27 usable D6 exposures and 18-25 D3 exposures. With neighbours modelled, every channel from 0.75 to 5.0 um is at or below zero, including the line wavelengths (Pa alpha, Br alpha, 4.50, Pf beta). Local noise from apertures on a grid is 11-15 mJy in D5/D6; that is confusion from crowding. Repeatability at the fixed place is 1-4 mJy for the aperture and 0.1-1 mJy for the forced fit.
findings.evidence: forced.json, Jul-Aug 2025 values -2.5..+0.1 mJy in all D3-D6 channels (D6 1.855 to 5.000 um listed). measurements.json grid_mad: D6 10.9/14.8/13.0, D5 14.9/14.8/14.9 mJy. The aperture MAD in faint visits is 0.8-3.8 mJy.

findings.what: The continuum is smooth and red. It is flat in F_nu at about 100-110 mJy from 3.6 to 5 um, falls to about 20 mJy at 1.7 um and about 1-3 mJy at 1.2 um, and is below about 0.5 mJy under 1.1 um. A blackbody of about 1150 K, a reddened blackbody of about 1270 K, or a flat F_nu with A_K about 1.9 all describe it to 5-8 per cent per point; the shape cannot tell them apart. There is no clear ice absorption: 3.0 um is not depressed. The single channel at the CO2-ice wavelength (4.262 um) is 35 per cent low, and the next one (4.298 um) is 2.2x high, unidentified. Both are single exposures and inconclusive.
findings.evidence: spectrum2.py fits to 69 continuum channels (Feb-Mar 2026, forced fluxes, 5 per cent + 1 mJy errors). Blackbody: T 1147 +/- 17 K, chi2/dof 317/67 = 4.7. Blackbody x extinction (Indebetouw 2005 law): T 1270 +/- 113 K, A_K 0.5 +/- 0.4, 4.7. Flat F_nu x extinction: A_K 1.87 +/- 0.07, 4.9. Data/model 0.92-1.05 in D2-D6. The faint visits have no measurable continuum to fit; the raw-aperture fit (T 2100 K) describes the neighbour stars, not the candidate.

pixels.could_not_check: (a) I did not read the SPHEREx Explanatory Supplement's description of ghost geometry; ghosts were tested empirically instead. (b) The images were checked directly only for ghosts of V345 Nor; ghosts of other bright stars (for example the 98 Jy star 24.6 arcmin S) were not tested in images. They are covered only by the argument that the source keeps one sky place under both orientations (Aug 2026 line detections) and while crossing the detector. (c) Big cutouts were fetched for D5/D6 only, not D1-D4. (d) Identifications of the 4.30, 4.49 and 4.73-4.77 um features and of He I 1.083 um are tentative; the D1 1.082 um point comes from an exposure whose aperture holds PERSIST-flagged pixels. (e) Whether this is a known or already-reported nova (VSX, CBAT/ATel/TNS nova lists) is outside this lens and was not searched. (f) The absolute level of the forced fit has a bias of about -0.7 mJy, judged from the 2025 values. The +2-5 mJy D4-D6 continuum residual in Jul-Sep 2026 is at the level of the method's systematics. (g) The April D6 flux rests on 3 clean core pixels next to a snowball patch. (h) Time and spectrum are mixed in Feb-Mar: each detector observed on different days (D4 Feb 21-24, D5 Feb 24-27, D6 Feb 28-Mar 3), so variability within those 10 days cannot be separated from spectral shape.

pixels.summary:
Candidate C survives the pixel and instrument attack: it is a real point source fixed on the sky. Its sky position stays put to 0.14/0.18 arcsec over 47 exposures in 4 detectors, while it lands across most of the detector (x 885-1893, y 47-1926 px). It sits in the same place again in Aug 2026, when the spacecraft is turned about 175 deg. It is shaped like a star and is detected at the same instant in paired detectors (D3 with D6, D2 with D5). It is not a ghost of the 607 Jy Mira V345 Nor 7.7 arcmin north: nothing appears where such a ghost would fall in the other visits (-0.9..-0.3 mJy against at least 60 expected). It is not persistence, crosstalk, a mover or a calibration jump (comparison stars are normal in the key exposures). I reproduced the sweep's medians.

Corrections to the write-up:
- The true centroid is 3.0 arcsec from the sweep's position. The GLIMPSE '4.1 arcsec counterpart' is 6.2 arcsec away, so nothing catalogued lies within 6 arcsec; the Hi-GAL clump is 3.6 arcsec away.
- The 178 and 300 mJy tile values are emission-line channels; the continuum is about 105 mJy.
- The 4-12 mJy faint-state values are neighbour light. The candidate itself is at or below 0 mJy in Jul-Aug 2025 in every channel.
- It was still about a third as bright on 9-10 April 2026.
- It is not 'back to nearly nothing' in Aug 2026: the continuum has faded but emission lines (4.49 um, Br alpha, 4.65-4.70 um) are still detected at the same place.

The spectrum is a smooth red continuum (about 1150 K blackbody, or reddened, chi2/dof about 4.7) under very strong hydrogen lines. That looks like a heavily reddened classical nova more than a young-star flare. The nova-list / 'already reported' check by the other lenses therefore decides novelty; my lens cannot.

Note for the lead agent: the user's latest message ('WHY IS THIS KEEPING ON CHANGING, IT IS NOT EVEN VISIBLE') seems to be about the app, and this vetting step does not address it.

findings.what: NEUTRAL: NEOWISE's only detection near the place in 2010 to 2024 is an artefact. On 2022-03-02 (frame 37024r163, MJD 59640.183) one exposure shows W2 10.69 (9.1 mJy) 2.1" from the 2026 position. W1 sees nothing in the same exposure (SNR -4.4). It is absent in the other 14 exposures of that visit, including those 1.6 h before and after. Its PSF fit is poor (w2rchi2 8.8). The pixel mask shows bit 1 (static noisy pixel) and bit 28 ('positive or negative spike-outlier', per the WISE Explanatory Supplement table I read) on a 2x2 pixel block at the spot. So it is not an earlier outburst. The chance of a stray spurious detection landing this close is about 1.5 to 7%.

Within 10': 189 objects, including about 20 SPICY YSO candidates, ATLASGAL young stars, dense cores, bubbles, long-period variable candidates, Miras, Cepheids and eclipsing binaries. No maser, planetary nebula, supernova remnant, nova or cataclysmic variable. This fits an embedded young star, but it is not proof.

archives.summary:
For this lens the claim holds: before 2025 nothing was at the place that comes close to the 2026 brightness. There are two corrections and one open lead.

Correction one: the counterpart is misidentified. My own centroid from 41 bright-epoch SPHEREx exposures (astrometry tied to AllWISE) puts the flare 3.0\" south of the sweep position. That is 6\" from the GLIMPSE [4.5] 13.8 star the sweep calls the counterpart, so that star is excluded.

What was there before, at the corrected position:
- Nearest catalogued sources: faint VVV stars at 1.9\" to 2.2\" (Ks 17.3 and 16.9, not variable from 2010 to 2019) and a Deep GLIMPSE [3.6] 15.5 source at 2.7\".
- Closest of all: a faint red point source in DECaPS2 at 0.9\" (z_AB about 21.2, r about 23.5) that no catalogue lists. It could be the object at rest or an unrelated star; this is the lead.

Upper limits, checked against neighbours of known brightness and by looking at the images:
- 3.6 to 4.5 um: no more than 0.2 to 0.4 mJy in Spitzer images from before 2007, before 2015 and before 2018.
- 4.6 um: nothing of 5 mJy or more in any of 23 WISE/NEOWISE half-year visits from 2010 to March 2024; a 5.2 mJy star 11\" away is seen in essentially every exposure.
- 2.2 um: no more than about 0.1 mJy in VVV, 2010 to 2019.
- 24 um: no more than 4.4 mJy (MIPSGAL, 2006). 22 um: no more than about 21 mJy (WISE, 2010). 70 um: under 0.13 Jy.

Correction two: NEOWISE's only nearby detection (one W2-only exposure on 2022-03-02, 2.1\" away) falls on a pixel the mask flags as a noisy pixel with a spike outlier. It is an artefact, not an earlier outburst.

Brightening: my own photometry on the cached cutouts gives about 118 mJy in D6 and 54 mJy in D3 in Feb-Mar 2026. Against the limits above, that is at least about 20x since every half-year visit up to March 2024, at least 270 to 560x against Spitzer at 4.5 um, and at least about 340x at 2.2 um.

Known object or already reported: no variable-star or transient catalogue I could reach lists anything within 11.8\". The place lies inside a cold Hi-GAL clump that is dark at 70 um, on the edge of an infrared-dark cloud, which fits an outburst of an embedded young star (context only).

Not checked: SkyMapper, ASAS-SN, the DECaPS catalogues, unTimely, VVV images and 2MASS images, because their services failed or gave no answer that passed a control.

Each of those searches found a control object where one exists. The nearest catalogued variable is a Gaia RS star 13 arcsec away with 0.1 mag amplitude, and the nearest object from any paper is 2.67 deg away. I did not reproduce the brightening; that is outside this lens.

Caveats:
- SIMBAD's control failed: the Harvard mirror does not have the 2025 novae, and CDS was down.
- TNS does not list V7994 Sgr, so it is not complete for Galactic novae.
- ATel full text was refused (robot check) and ADS needed a token, so a report that gives the position only in a telegram body or a paper could be missed.
- No other survey covered this embedded spot in early 2026: Gaia alerts had ended, ZTF cannot reach Dec -52, Fink shows no Rubin alerts there, and the microlensing surveys watch other fields. A report would not be expected even if the flare is real, so 'not reported' says nothing about whether it is real.

ordinary.lens: Ordinary explanations, and what it probably is. I checked for a Solar System body, a catalogued variable or eruptive object, glare or a ghost of a bright star, a calibration fault in one detector, and the physical class.

C's width in D5/D6 equals the stars' (ratio 1.00 to 1.09). C sits at the same place in Aug 2026 but not in Aug 2025, which matters if the ghost depends on roll angle. ordinary.summary:
C survives this lens, with caveats. It is a real astrophysical transient. It is not a Solar System body: it holds one sky position to 0.2 arcsec over 13 days and again 5.6 months later, and JPL sb_ident lists nothing near it on any date while the same request finds Pallas. It is not a calibration fault: the rise is smooth across all detectors, and field stars in the line exposures stay steady. It is not a ghost of the bright Mira V345 Nor, 7.8 arcmin away: wrong spectrum, star-like width, and it reappears in Aug 2026. Nothing catalogued as variable, eruptive, maser, PN, YSO, OH/IR or X-ray lies within 1 arcmin.

I reproduced the brightening with my own photometry. With a 9.2-arcsec aperture the place is about 0 to 2 mJy in Jul-Aug 2025. In Feb-Mar 2026 the continuum is about 85 to 105 mJy at 4 to 5 um. In Jul-Sep 2026 it is about 3 to 5 mJy.

Corrections to the sweep's write-up:
- The position is off by 2.84 arcsec. The true one is RA 241.709051, Dec -52.205612. At that position GLIMPSE's 'counterpart' is 6.0 arcsec away and the nearest VVV star (Ks 16.9, steady 2010-2019) is 1.9 to 2.0 arcsec away. No progenitor is detected, so the rise is at least about 6.5 mag in Ks and at least 5 mag at 4.5 um.
- Its two bright tile images fell on emission lines (Pf-beta at 4.631 um, and a feature at 4.739 um).

What it probably is: an ordinary classical nova hidden behind dust, not the young-star flare the sweep suggests.
- In Feb-Mar 2026 the spectrum shows strong H I recombination lines with very large EWs (Pa-alpha peak 10 times its continuum, Br-alpha 4.7 times). The continuum is very red: about 1,150 K unreddened, or hotter if reddened.
- By Aug 2026 the continuum has faded about 30 times (0.7 to 0.8 mag/month at 2 to 5 um). A line at 4.488 um, which I read as [Mg IV] (80 to 109 eV ionisation), now dominates at 10.7 times the continuum; it was absent in Feb-Mar.
- This is the infrared evolution of a classical nova moving into its coronal phase. Evans and Gehrz 2012 list [Mg IV] 4.4867 as a nova coronal line. This project's own SPHEREx spectra of the known novae V462 Lup and V1935 Cen show the same 4.47 to 4.51 um feature.

Ranking:
1. Obscured classical nova, erupted between Aug 2025 and Feb 2026.
2. Eruptive YSO (EXor-like) in the Hi-GAL clump 3.75 arcsec away. Its only support is the location. Against it: [Mg IV], line EWs of thousands of Angstrom, at least 6.5 mag in Ks, no infrared progenitor, and more than 26 Lsun at the clump distance.
3. X-ray binary outburst, not excluded.

Excluded: FU Ori-type (it faded within months and shows emission lines), luminous red nova (high-ionisation lines), symbiotic, R CrB or dusty giant (no bright progenitor), Mira or OH/IR (not in AllWISE), microlensing (chromatic, and lines come and go).

The deciding observation: a 1 to 2.5 um spectrum now at R of 1,000 or more. A nova shows broad (1,000 km/s or more) H I and He I lines and coronal lines such as [Si VI] 1.964 or [Si VII] 2.483 um. A YSO shows narrow Br-gamma and CO 2.29 um bandheads. A supersoft X-ray detection would also settle it for a nova.

Call it a candidate, not a discovery. I did not check TNS or ATel systematically, so an existing report is not ruled out. The app and the user's complaint about the page changing were outside this step, and I changed no repository file.
